description_full: American Tower Corporation one of the largest global REITs, is a leading independent owner, operator and developer of multitenant communications real estate with a portfolio of over 147,000 communications sites and a highly interconnected footprint of U.S. data center facilities. American Tower Corporation was incorporated in 1995 in Delaware and is based in Massachusetts, Boston.
ceo_bio: Mr. Steven O. Vondran J.D. | President, CEO & Director | Age 54 | Compensation: $3.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $2.2M ranks in the below the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 12%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $778K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $36K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: American Tower Corporation (REI is a large-cap real estate business with a $87.6B market cap on $10.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -0% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $3.8B in free cash flow — roughly 36 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.6×.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 46% operating margin runs 23pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.28x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 3.0% of sector revenue and 6.8% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.08 vs 5y 0.59), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $454.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 56% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $142 (margin of safety -33%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 49%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $92.32 to $213 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/FCF 23.1 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 30% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $216 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 0pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).
It converts 36% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.16x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 36%.
ROE of 69% is amplified by 17.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.5B of cash against $37.2B of debt), with interest covered 3.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.22 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.40 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.2% over 3 years, 5.8% over 5 years and 8.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 5.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue down 62% and FFO growth of 7.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 15.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 40, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 97%.
Insider trading is two-way: 5 purchases and 11 sales over the past year, net $7.6M sold.
It returns 4.0% a year to shareholders (0.4% in buybacks and 3.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 10.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,866 employees, each generates about $2.2M of revenue, in line with the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 12.0% a year.
That works out to $778K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.3M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
